Some of these patients have been initially misdiagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome, postmononucleosis syndrome, chronic Lyme disease, or psychiatric disorders (depression or anorexia nervosa).
A severe dietary imbalance, such as in anorexia nervosa and in war or famine conditions, also can cause pellagra.

faq.a: BMI reflects overall energy deficit and correlates with risk of cardiac and metabolic complications.
faq.q: Why is BMI used for severity staging?

faq.a: Yes; nutritional rehabilitation and psychotherapy are first‑line; medication is added after weight restoration if needed.
faq.q: Can anorexia be treated without medication?

faq.a: A rapid shift of electrolytes when feeding starts; prevent by starting low calories, supplementing phosphate, potassium and thiamine, and monitoring labs daily.
faq.q: What is re‑feeding syndrome and how to prevent it?

exam: What immediate investigations are required for a patient with BMI 14 kg/m² and bradycardia? — ECG, electrolytes, renal function, and cardiac monitoring to assess for arrhythmia and re‑feeding risk.

How would you differentiate anorexia nervosa from chronic TB in a low‑resource setting? — Look for fever, night sweats, cough, positive sputum GeneXpert; TB has systemic signs, whereas anorexia shows body‑image preoccupation.

A patient with anorexia is about to start re‑feeding; what electrolyte abnormality are you most concerned about and why? — Phosphate depletion; its rapid rise can cause cardiac failure and respiratory collapse.
Why are SSRIs not first‑line in acute anorexia nervosa? — They are ineffective until weight is restored and may worsen nausea; psychotherapy and nutrition take priority.

Explain the role of family‑based therapy for adolescent anorexia in a rural hospital. — Engages caregivers to supervise meals, improves adherence, and is feasible where specialist services are scarce.
What red‑flag sign would prompt transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Persistent QTc >500 ms or refractory electrolyte abnormalities despite correction.

How does HIV infection modify the presentation of anorexia nervosa? — HIV can cause weight loss and appetite loss, masking the psychological component; screen for opportunistic infections and consider ART interactions.
Describe the key components of monitoring during the first week of re‑feeding. — Daily weight, electrolytes (phosphate, potassium, magnesium), vital signs, and ECG for QT changes.
ai.title: Anorexia Nervosa
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Anorexia nervosa is a severe eating disorder characterised by self‑induced weight loss, intense fear of gaining weight and body‑image disturbance. Diagnosis relies on DSM‑5/ICD‑11 criteria; severity is staged by BMI. Management combines nutritional rehabilitation, psychotherapy and careful monitoring for medical complications.

b: DSM‑5 criteria: (1) Restriction of energy intake, (2) Low weight (BMI <18.5 for adults), (3) Intense fear of gaining weight, (4) Distorted body image.
ICD‑11: Similar criteria, emphasising ‘persistent restriction’ and ‘distorted perception of body shape.’
sections.p: Anorexia nervosa is defined by persistent restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, an intense fear of gaining weight, and a disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced.

b: Mild: BMI ≥17 kg/m²
Moderate: BMI 16–16.9 kg/m²
Severe: BMI 15–15.9 kg/m²
Extreme: BMI <15 kg/m²
sections.p: Severity is graded by body‑mass index (BMI) for adults and by percent median BMI for adolescents.

b: Psychological: perfectionism, overvalued ideas about thinness, family conflict.
Sociocultural: media ideals, peer pressure, stigma about body size.
Medical triggers common in East Africa: HIV‑related weight loss, chronic TB, malaria‑associated anorexia, post‑infectious fatigue, anemia, and use of herbal appetite suppressants.
sections.p: Anorexia is multifactorial; psychosocial pressures are most common, but in low‑resource settings additional medical contributors must be considered.

b: Visible thinness, lanugo hair, cold intolerance, bradycardia.
Restrictive eating, excessive exercise, purging in the binge‑purge subtype.
Psychiatric comorbidity: depression, anxiety, obsessive‑compulsive traits.
sections.p: Patients often present with marked weight loss, preoccupation with food, ritualised eating patterns, and denial of the seriousness of their low weight.
Investigations aim to assess medical complications and rule out mimics.

t.b: Confirms low body weight and tracks response to re‑feeding.
Detects anemia, leukopenia (common with HIV/TB) – treat underlying infection if present.
Identifies hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis (purging), hepatic stress – correct before re‑feeding.
Euthyroid sick syndrome is common; abnormal results may reflect severity, not primary thyroid disease.
Looks for bradycardia, QT prolongation – guides safe re‑feeding and need for cardiac monitoring.

t.a: HIV, TB screening (sputum GeneXpert, chest X‑ray)
t.b: Excludes infectious causes of weight loss; if unavailable, use clinical risk assessment and treat empirically when indicated.

b: Cardiac: bradycardia <40 bpm, hypotension, arrhythmias.
Electrolyte: severe hypokalaemia (<2.5 mmol/L), phosphate <0.5 mmol/L.
Re‑feeding syndrome: rapid rise in phosphate after nutrition.
Severe dehydration, renal failure, liver transaminase >3× ULN.
Suicidal ideation or self‑harm.
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.

b: Medical: monitor vitals, correct electrolytes, treat infections (e.g., start anti‑TB therapy if active TB).
Nutritional: start low‑calorie re‑feeding (≈30‑40 kcal/kg/day), increase slowly, monitor for re‑feeding syndrome.
Pharmacology: SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine) are useful after weight restoration; avoid antipsychotics solely for weight gain unless psychosis present.
Psychotherapy: family‑based therapy (FBT) for adolescents, CBT‑E (cognitive‑behavioural therapy for eating disorders) for adults.
Avoid: high‑dose benzodiazepines (risk of respiratory depression) and stimulant appetite suppressants.
sections.p: Management is multidisciplinary: medical stabilisation, nutritional rehabilitation, and psychotherapy.

b: Regular weight checks, electrolyte monitoring every 1–2 weeks until stable.
Psychiatric review every 4–6 weeks; adjust therapy as needed.
Community outreach: address body‑image pressures, promote healthy nutrition in schools.
sections.p: Long‑term follow‑up reduces relapse; education of families and schools is key.

b: Chronic infection (HIV, TB, malaria) causing weight loss – look for fever, night sweats, positive microbiology.
Depression with loss of appetite – predominant low mood, lack of body‑image preoccupation.
Hyperthyroidism – weight loss with tachycardia, heat intolerance, elevated TSH‑free T4.
Normal BMI in early disease may hide severe malnutrition; use percent median BMI for adolescents.
Electrolytes can appear normal if patient has recently purged and re‑hydrated; repeat testing.
ECG QT interval may be normal at rest but prolongs with re‑feeding; continuous monitoring recommended.
sections.p: Lab and clinical findings may be deceptive.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe bradycardia (<40 bpm) or hypotension (systolic <90 mmHg)
Signs of re‑feeding syndrome (rapid rise in phosphate, edema)
